Definite, repeating, long range order of particles. Definite characteristic shape. Sharp and fixed melting point. Breaks along a definite plane, giving smooth surfaces. A definite value of heat of fusion. Examples: NaCl, diamond.

Irregular; only short range order. Irregular shape. Softens gradually over a range of temperature. Breaks irregularly. No definite value of heat of fusion. Examples: glass, rubber, pitch. a c b alpha: between b and c beta: between a and c gamma: between a and b 6 lattice parameters: a, b, c, alpha, beta, gamma The six lattice parameters: three edge lengths and three angles between them. a b c a: bottom edge, b: side edge, c: left edge of the unit cell one unit cell, highlighted The crystal is built by stacking unit cells together, one highlighted here.

A crystal consists of a basic structural unit, or motif, repeated in three dimensions. The basic unit may be a single atom, molecule or ion, or a group of atoms or molecules, which has an identical environment throughout the crystal. It is also called the basis of the crystal. A basis has the same stoichiometric composition as the crystal itself. The lattice, or space lattice, is the geometrical idealisation of the structure. It is obtained by placing a point at the same location of each basis in the crystal; the resulting three-dimensional distribution of points in space forms the lattice. A
A unit cell is described by six numbers: a, b, c , the lengths of the three edges, and α, β, γ , the angles between the edges (α between b and c, β between a and c, γ between a and b).

A symmetry operation is a movement of a crystal after which it looks exactly the same as before. The imaginary point, line or plane about which the operation is carried out is called a symmetry element. Proper rotation axes (n-fold). Rotation by 360°/n about an axis leaves the crystal unchanged. Only 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6-fold axes are possible in a periodic crystal. A 5-fold axis (and 7, 8-fold) can never exist in a crystal, because space cannot be filled by repeating a pentagon without leaving gaps. Plane of symmetry (m). An imaginary plane that divides the crystal into two halves, each a mirror

Ca 2+ ions are arranged at the corners and at the centres of the faces of a cubic unit cell, and F − ions are at the centres of the eight small cubes into which the cell may be divided. Each Ca 2+ is coordinated by 8 F − neighbours at the corners of a cube, while each F − has 4 Ca 2+ neighbours. This is the only structure in the notes with 8:4 coordination. The reverse structure, antifluorite, is taken by oxides such as Li 2 O and Na 2 O, with the cation and anion positions exchanged. (Standard material added here; it is not in the notes.) The unit cell of the rutile lattice is a given figure. The cation is octahedrally surrounded by six anions, while the anion (O 2− ) is trigonally surrounded by three cations. Rutile has a low-symmetry anion sublattice that fits neither a simple cubic nor an fcc lattice. The cation sublattice is a distorted body-centred cube, because one side of the cube differs from the others, the cation sublattice is actually body-centred tetragonal. The unit cell is tetragonal.

Named after the mineral CaTiO 3 . O 2− ions, along with the larger cation (Ca 2+ ), form a ccp and fcc array in which the octahedral holes formed by O 2− are occupied by the smaller cation (Ti 4+ ). In the unit cell, the eight corners of the cube are occupied by Ca 2+ , O 2− are placed at the centres of the six faces, and Ti 4+ is placed at the centre of the cube. Named after the mineral ilmenite. It adopts the structure of corundum (α-Al 2 O 3 ). In a hexagonal close-packed array of O 2− ions, two-thirds of the octahedral holes are occupied, one-third by Fe 2+ and one-third by Ti 4+ , in alternating layers. Named after the mineral spinel, MgAl 2 O 4 . It consists of a ccp array of oxide ions in which the divalent metal ion (Mg 2+ ) occupies 1/8 of the tetrahedral holes and the trivalent metal ion (Al 3+ ) occupies 1/2 of the octahedral holes. In a ccp anion sublattice there is one octahedral hole and two tetrahedral holes per anion. There are four oxides per formula unit, and consequently four octahedral holes and eight tetrahedral holes. Normal: (A II ) tet (B III ) 2oct O 4

In an inverse spinel, half of the B ions occupy 1/8 of the tetrahedral holes, and A and the other half of B occupy 1/2 of the octahedral holes in the ccp array of O 2− . In an inverse spinel the A 2+ ion has a strong tendency to occupy octahedral holes, which is why the B 3+ ion is displaced into the tetrahedral hole.
